headline: Peru's Technical and Operational Analysis Committee has determined that the South Korean K2 Black Panther is the best option for the country's next main battle tank, recommending it for acquisition by the Peruvian Army. During the evaluation process, the K2 outperformed the German Leopard 2A6, the American M1A1/A2 Abrams, the Chinese VT-4, as well as competing offers from Poland and Türkiye. The procurement program calls for the acquisition of 150 tanks to replace the T-55 and AMX-13, both of which have been in service for more than 50 years. The first 46 tanks will be manufactured in South Korea, while the remaining vehicles are planned to be assembled at a new facility in Peru. Construction of the plant is part of Hyundai Rotem's proposal, which includes a $270 million investment and the use of 30% locally sourced components. Last year, the Peruvian Army signed a framework agreement with Hyundai Rotem covering technology cooperation and the potential joint production of K2 tanks and K808 armored vehicles. In addition, on July 11, the vessel GLOVIS SAFETY delivered at least two K2 tanks and six K808 armored vehicles to the Port of Callao for trials under local climatic conditions.

headline: A Ukrainian FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile flying at extremely low altitude during one of the missile strikes on Russia. The exact date, location, and other details remain unknown. The footage illustrates how low these missiles can fly, making them much harder to detect and intercept using conventional ground-based radar and air defense systems. This is where airborne early warning and control (AEW&C) aircraft play a critical role. Russia could face growing challenges if Ukraine significantly expands production of these cruise missiles or acquires long-range cruise missiles from Western countries. The Russian Aerospace Forces (VKS) operate a limited number of AEW&C aircraft, making it difficult to maintain continuous radar coverage over such a vast territory and respond effectively to repeated large-scale cruise missile attacks.

headline: One vessel to watch is the Bahamas-flagged, Qatar-owned Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) carrier Al Areesh. Automatic Information System (AIS) data from http://MarineTraffic.com indicates the vessel has now reached the U.S. enforced naval blockade line at the entrance to the Gulf of Oman twice. After transiting outbound through the Strait of Hormuz on July 29 using Iran's traffic separation scheme, Al Areesh reached the apparent blockade line before reversing course back into the Gulf of Oman. It has now returned to the blockade line, but rather than continuing seaward or turning back again, is loitering in a north-south pattern along the blockade line. The vessel's movements are noteworthy because as a Bahamas-flagged, Qatar owned LNG carrier outbound from the Persian Gulf, it does not appear to fall within the publicly stated scope of the U.S. blockade, which U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) has described as restricting commercial traffic supporting Iran. If U.S. forces are delaying or preventing the vessel from departing the Gulf, the rationale is currently unclear. Alternatively, the vessel may be awaiting routing instructions, clearance, or a commercial decision by its operator. AIS data alone cannot determine the reason for its current behavior.

headline: Spain is facing its most serious migration crisis in years after a mass surge into the North African enclave of Ceuta left at least 72 people dead and reignited debate over European border security. According to Spanish authorities, more than 50,000 people attempted to enter Ceuta from Morocco by land and sea, overwhelming local resources. While the vast majority have since returned to Morocco, Spanish officials continue to recover bodies, reinforce the border, and investigate the role of human smuggling networks and online misinformation in fueling the surge. The crisis has prompted a broader European response. Twenty-two EU member states have called for stronger external border protections, Spain has installed a 500-meter floating sea barrier off Ceuta, and Italy temporarily reinstated border controls with Spain, citing security concerns. Until this incident, Spain had actually experienced a decline in irregular migration during 2026. Through the end of June, 12,138 migrants had entered Spain irregularly; 32% fewer than during the same period in 2025. Arrivals to the Canary Islands were down sharply, while land crossings into Ceuta and Melilla had already increased by more than 150% year-over-year, foreshadowing mounting pressure along Spain's North African land border. Image: Wall Street Journal

headline: Ukraine's long-range drone campaign appears to have struck another Wildberries distribution center, this time in Novosyomyeikino, continuing a sustained effort to target Russia's largest e-commerce and logistics network. According to Russian officials, the strike ignited a fire at the facility. This video from Telegram purportedly shows a massive fire at the facility following the earlier Ukrainian drone strike. Wildberries is essentially Russia's equivalent of Amazon, operating the country's largest online marketplace with an extensive nationwide warehousing and distribution network. Ukraine argues the company supports Russia's war effort by selling dual-use goods and equipment used by the military, an allegation Moscow denies. The attack is the latest in a broader campaign that has targeted roughly a dozen Wildberries facilities since mid-July, disrupting an estimated 10% of the company's logistics capacity and forcing the retailer to reroute shipments, compensate victims, and absorb significant financial losses.
